title: Applicable codes (L&I)
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: Beginning July 1, 2026 Philadelphia adopts the 2021 ICC family of codes with local amendments (intro).
Table: Philadelphia Electrical Code = 2020 National Electric Code (table row).
Accessibility provisions of the 2018 I-Codes apply; 2021 accessibility provisions under the PA Construction Code Act are rescinded (footnote 1).

title: Code Bulletin B-2501: Implementation of 2021 International Codes for Philadelphia
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: Issued October 20, 2025 by the Chief Code Official (p.1 header).
PA DLI's adoption of the 2021 I-Codes under the PA Construction Code Act (Act 45 of 1999) takes effect January 1, 2026 (p.1 Background).
Adopted referenced standards include 2020 NFPA 70 (NEC) and 2019 NFPA 72 (p.2 Policy).

Applications received before July 1, 2026 could choose 2018 or 2021 editions (default 2018 if not specified); all applications received on or after July 1, 2026, including trade permits, must comply with the 2021 codes (p.2 Permit Application Review Timeline).
Amendments to issued permits stay on the original edition; expired and resubmitted permits go to 2021 codes (p.2 Additional Considerations).
The Philadelphia Administrative Code continues as a local construction code within the UCC (p.2).
notes: Practical meaning: before 2026 Philadelphia work under the 2018 codes used the 2017 NEC; since 2026-07-01 the 2020 NEC (via 2021 IBC/IRC/IEBC) is mandatory.

title: FAQ PB-021: What Code Applies to Electrical Work?
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: Electrical work is governed by the Building, Residential and Existing Building Codes; NFPA 70 applies only as explicitly referenced, and where they conflict the Building Codes govern (p.1 Answer).
Residential (detached 1-2 family or townhouse up to 3 stories) electrical work is governed by Part VIII of the Philadelphia Residential Code; work not covered there must meet NFPA 70 (p.2).
Non-residential new work: Building Code Ch. 27 references NFPA 70; repairs/alterations/change of occupancy use the Existing Building Code (p.2).
Legally installed existing systems need not be upgraded unless explicitly required; new work must meet current standards (p.1 principles).
notes: Dated February 2024 (pre-2021 code adoption) but the framework is edition-neutral.

title: 2021 Code Implementation - Electrical (L&I webinar slides)
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: PA UCC amends IRC E3601.8 so the outdoor emergency disconnect applies only to one- and two-family detached dwellings; in Philadelphia it does not apply to rowhomes/townhouses up to 3 stories but does apply to detached buildings, twins, duplexes and rowhomes over 3 stories (p.19).
Surge protection (230.67 / E3606.5) required on all dwelling-unit services (p.20).

PA UCC keeps the 2018 island countertop rule: one receptacle for islands 24x12 in or larger in single-family dwellings up to 3 stories; larger/multi-family kitchens follow the 2020 NEC area-based rule (p.24).
PA UCC keeps 2015-style foyer rule for IRC dwellings: foyers >60 sq ft need a receptacle on each wall 6 ft or wider, minimum one (p.25).
GFCI expanded to 250 V receptacles, all basements and indoor damp/wet locations; all outdoor outlets at dwellings need GFCI (pp.27-30).
TIA 20-19 postponed GFCI for HVAC equipment until September 1, 2026; L&I extends it to Residential Code buildings (p.31).
Air-sealed (NEMA OS 4) electrical boxes required in the building thermal envelope (p.34).
New EVITP requirement: from July 2026 electrical permits for EV charger installation/repair go only to contractors whose license includes EVITP (or approved equivalent) certification (p.37).
notes: Presentation dated ~mid 2025; implementation dates on slides (Sept 2025/March 2026) were estimates and were superseded by B-2501 (Jan 1 / July 1, 2026).

title: 2021 I-Code Local Changes (L&I summary, May 2026)
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: Lists Philadelphia ordinances amending the 2021 codes: Admin (Bill 260393), Building (260394), IECC residential (250644), Mechanical (260391), Plumbing (250645), Residential (260395) (pp.1-6).
R-E3901.4.2.1 reintroduces peninsular countertops and islands in kitchen receptacle requirements as in the 2018 IRC, because the PA UCC did not account for peninsulas (p.6).

Local IECC changes: 100% high-efficacy lamps, dimmer/occupancy-sensor controls for permanently installed lighting, auto shut-off for exterior lighting >30 W, exterior lighting limits for multifamily (pp.2-3).
Mechanical change removes previous A2L machinery-room language tied to NFPA 70 hazardous-location requirements (p.3 M-1106.4).
No separate electrical-subcode (Subcode E) amendment appears in the list (pp.1-6).
notes: Says 'changes to be adopted' - enactment status of each bill not individually verified.

title: FAQ PB-037: Does my project require an emergency disconnect?
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: Emergency disconnect (2020 NEC 230.85 / 2021 IRC E3601.8) is triggered by all new services and existing service upgrades, e.g., 100 A to 200 A (p.1 Answer 1).
Not required for rowhouses/townhomes (three or more attached) up to three stories; required for detached single-family and twins (p.1).

Common Philadelphia condition: underground service entering through the basement floor with interior meters; four compliant configurations shown; conductors under 2 in of concrete count as outside (230.6); infeasible cases need a Board of Building Standards variance (pp.3-6).

title: Get an Electrical Permit
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: An Electrical Permit is required for installation, alteration, renewal, replacement or repair of electrical and communication systems; a separate PECO service and meter application may be needed (Service overview).

EZ (no-plans) permits: 1-2 family work under 200 A connected load and <=600 V; services <=200 A; commercial interior alterations under 2,000 sq ft; like-for-like equipment replacement; low-voltage; temporary wiring; EV chargers meeting the EVC standard (EZ permits).

Per Title 4 A-301.2.3 no permit is needed for minor maintenance such as replacing lamps, breakers, fuses, switches, sockets, ballasts, receptacles, and like-for-like light fixtures; low-voltage wiring in 1-2 family and Group U is also exempt (Projects that may not need permits).
A licensed electrical contractor must perform all electrical work, with active license, current city taxes and insurance on file (Contractor).
Third-party inspection: the owner or agent must hire a licensed electrical inspection agency to perform all inspections (Third-party inspection).
From July 1, 2026 a permit including an EV charger requires EVITP certification on the contractor's license (EV Charger Certification Required).
Rough-in approval allows cable/conduit/box/service equipment before full permit; valid 60 days; work may not be concealed (Rough-in Permits).
Electrical Permit is not issued until any required Building Permit is issued (Related permits).

title: Get an Electrical Contractor License
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: Required to do electrical work in Philadelphia, including low-voltage wiring (Service overview).
Experience: at least 4 years of electrical work for a company licensed by a local or state jurisdiction; 2 years of electrical education = 1 year, up to 2 years substitution (Experience).

Must pass the Philadelphia Electrical Contractor Examination administered by the International Code Council; apply within 12 months of passing or the exam must reference the current Philadelphia Code (Testing and certification).
8 hours of NFPA 70 coursework (current or later edition) from a PA DLI-approved provider within 12 months before application (Continuing education).
Insurance: GL $500,000/occurrence, auto $300,000, workers' comp $100k/$100k/$500k (Insurance).
Also needs BIRT tax ID and Commercial Activity License; fee $262 (incl. $60 application fee), renewal $202 (Requirements/Cost).
EVITP certification needed for EV charger work; mandatory on permits from July 1, 2026 (Electric vehicle infrastructure specialty).
notes: Proof of licensure in another jurisdiction may count as experience proof subject to L&I approval; no exam reciprocity is described.

title: Get an Electrical Inspection Agency License
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: Companies need this license to perform inspections on work done under Philadelphia electrical permits; agencies must employ licensed electrical inspectors (Service overview).
At least one principal must have held a Philadelphia Electrical Inspector's License for at least one year; GL insurance $1,000,000 per occurrence (Requirements).
notes: Confirms Philadelphia's private third-party electrical inspection model.

title: Information sheet PB-010: Pre-Authorization of Multiple Electrical Service Connections
publisher: City of Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections
keyFacts: L&I pre-authorization of multiple services is often required for a PECO electrical service application; determinations only via an Electrical Permit or Preliminary Plan Review application (p.1).
Philadelphia Fire Department Fire Code Unit must acknowledge multiple-service conditions (p.1).
Capacity condition: additional services allowed above 2000 A at 1000 V or less, with engineer letter (p.2).
notes: Rev 10.2023 cites 2017 NEC 230.2; may be updated for the 2020 NEC - check for a newer revision.

title: State Board of Electrical Licensure (PA Department of State, BPOA)
publisher: Pennsylvania Department of State, Bureau of Professional and Occupational Affairs
keyFacts: Act 108 of 2026 was signed October 22, 2026, establishing the State Board of Electrical Licensure (page body).
The Act provides a two-year period before licensure requirements take effect (page body).
notes: No statewide electrician license exists yet; local licenses (e.g., Philadelphia) still control. Act text not retrieved (palegis.us returned empty pages to automated fetch).

title: What Electrical Contractors Need to Know About PA's New Statewide Electrical Licensure Law (law-firm summary)
keyFacts: Per this secondary summary: Act 108 of 2026 (Electrical Services Licensure Act) creates license classes for electrical contractors, electricians, residential electricians, apprentices and probationary workers.
Per this summary: contractor license needs age 23+, 10,000 documented hours, board exam and liability insurance; board regulations due in 18 months; licensure/enforcement starts after two years.

Per this summary: exam waiver for existing municipal license holders with 10,000 hours (electrician) or 6,000 hours (residential) or a registered apprenticeship, if they apply within the grandfathering window (window length stated inconsistently in the article).
notes: Third-party; verify against the enacted Act (SB 1260, 2025-26 session, palegis.us). Search snippets (not verified) say Section 501 licensure takes effect Oct 22, 2028 and reciprocity agreements are authorized.

title: Uniform Construction Code (PA Department of Labor & Industry)
keyFacts: UCC Triennial Update approved by IRRC October 16, 2025, published in the PA Bulletin November 8, 2025, effective January 1, 2026 (page body).
Commonwealth Court (Oct 26, 2022) permanently enjoined the 2021 accessibility updates; 2018 accessibility requirements still apply (page body).
Over 90% of PA's 2,562 municipalities administer and enforce the UCC locally or via certified third-party agencies (page body).
Previous 2018 I-Code regulations were effective February 14, 2022 (page body).
notes: The page does not itself name the NEC edition; per Philadelphia B-2501 the 2021 I-Codes reference the 2020 NEC.

title: PECO Application for Electric Service & Meter (S&M), form M-24175 Rev. 8/3-2024
keyFacts: All work must comply with PECO's Electric Tariff, Electric Service Requirements manual and Standards and be inspected by an approved inspection agency; Philadelphia requests may be shared with L&I (p.1 header).
PECO cannot commence work until all required information, including approved plans, is confirmed received (p.1).
Get service availability and meter location from PECO before buying equipment or wiring (p.1).
New residential construction: builder must trench for underground service at own expense per PECO standards (p.1).
notes: Utility form; read via fetch, not stored. The current PECO Electric Service Requirements ('Blue Book') manual URL was not found - gap.
